nodes.name: Whitebark pine
nodes.desc: A high-elevation pine whose large seeds feed nutcrackers, squirrels and bears. Blister rust, pine beetles and fire suppression threaten it, and it is listed as endangered in Canada.

nodes.name: Trembling aspen
nodes.desc: A deciduous tree of the valley floors. Young shoots are a spring favourite of elk, and heavy browsing can thin aspen groves.

nodes.name: Willows
nodes.desc: Streamside shrubs browsed by moose, elk and hares. Banff sources credit wolves with helping willow and aspen recover by keeping elk numbers in check.

nodes.name: Canadian buffaloberry
nodes.desc: A berry-bearing shrub of open forest. GloBI records show bears eating the berries and snowshoe hares eating the plant.

nodes.name: Rough fescue & montane grasses
nodes.desc: Bunchgrass of montane and foothill grassland that feeds elk, bighorn sheep and ground squirrels.

nodes.name: Clark's nutcracker
nodes.desc: The main disperser of whitebark pine. Each bird caches tens of thousands of seeds a year, and forgotten caches grow into new trees.

nodes.name: Red squirrel
nodes.desc: Cuts and stores conifer cones in middens that bears raid for seeds. It also eats birds and hares in GloBI records, and is itself prey for martens and coyotes.

nodes.name: Columbian Ground Squirrel
nodes.desc: A burrowing, hibernating squirrel of meadows and grassland that eats plants and is taken by coyotes and grizzlies.

nodes.name: Hoary marmot
nodes.desc: A large alpine ground squirrel that feeds on meadow plants in the short summer and hibernates. Grizzlies and coyotes prey on it.

nodes.name: Snowshoe hare
nodes.desc: Browses shrubs and twigs in forest and is a main prey of martens and coyotes.

nodes.name: Bighorn sheep
nodes.desc: Grazes grassy slopes and meadows and is prey for wolves, coyotes and grizzlies.

nodes.name: Moose
nodes.desc: Browses willow and aspen in wet valleys. Wolves and grizzlies are its main predators.

nodes.name: Elk
nodes.desc: Introduced to Banff in 1917 from Yellowstone. Grazes grasses and browses aspen, and large herds can degrade vegetation, so wolves are a key check on them.

nodes.name: Coyote
nodes.desc: Hunts hares, squirrels and marmots and scavenges elk carcasses, including at wolf kills.

nodes.name: American marten
nodes.desc: A forest weasel relative that hunts red squirrels and hares and also eats small rodents.

nodes.name: Common raven
nodes.desc: An intelligent scavenger that feeds on carrion left by wolves and other predators.

nodes.name: Gray wolf
nodes.desc: Returned to the Bow Valley in the 1980s and 1990s after being removed. Preys mainly on elk, moose and other hoofed animals.

nodes.name: Grizzly bear
nodes.desc: An omnivore that digs for squirrel and marmot burrows, eats berries and whitebark seeds, and takes young elk and moose. Parks Canada sources use it as a gauge of ecological integrity.

nodes.name: Snowpack & glacier meltwater
nodes.desc: Winter snow and glaciers feed the headwaters of major rivers rising in the mountains and water the valleys through summer.

nodes.name: Wildfire
nodes.desc: Fire renews aspen and montane grassland and stops shade-tolerant spruce and fir replacing whitebark pine. Decades of suppression changed the forests, and Parks Canada now uses prescribed burns.

nodes.name: Short mountain summer
nodes.desc: At high elevation the growing season is brief, so plants grow fast in summer and animals feed, store fat or hibernate.

nodes.name: Mountain soils
nodes.desc: Thin soils of valley floors and slopes that anchor the plants and are renewed by decomposers.

nodes.name: Fungi, insects & bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down dead wood, leaves and carcasses and return nutrients to the soil.
